description: Situations you hit on a team: merge, rebase, amend, reset, revert, cherry-pick, conflicts, and recovering with the reflog. Command behavior follows the Git documentation. Rewriting published history is the recurring hazard.

cards.front: What are the three places a change can live before it is committed?
cards.back: The working tree (files you edit), the index (what you staged with git add), and HEAD (the latest commit on this branch).
cards.explanation: Most 'I thought I committed that' bugs are a mix-up of these three. git diff shows working tree versus index. git diff --staged shows index versus HEAD. git status lists both. A commit snapshots the index, not whatever happens to be in the file if you edited after staging.
cards.example: Edit README, git add README, edit README again. The commit contains the staged version unless you add again.

cards.front: You committed on the wrong branch, and you have not pushed. How do you move that commit?
cards.back: Note the hash. git switch correct-branch, then git cherry-pick <hash>. Then remove it from the wrong branch with git switch wrong-branch and git reset --hard HEAD~1.
cards.explanation: reset --hard throws away that commit on the wrong branch. It is safe only because the cherry-pick made a copy and you have not pushed. If the wrong branch already had other unpushed work you want to keep, reset --hard is too blunt — use reset --soft or revert instead. cherry-pick copies the change. It does not move the original object until the original branch drops it.

cards.front: When is git commit --amend the right tool?
cards.back: When the commit is still private to you: you forgot a file, or the message is wrong, and you have not pushed (or nobody else has based work on it).
cards.explanation: Amend does not edit the old commit. It creates a new commit with a new hash and moves the branch pointer. Anyone who already pulled the old hash now has a divergent history. The Git docs warn about rewriting published commits for this reason. --amend reuses the previous message unless you pass -m or let the editor open. It also folds in whatever is currently staged.

cards.front: You amended a commit you had already pushed. What do teammates experience?
cards.back: Their next pull does not fast-forward. Your rewritten commit and their copy of the old commit have diverged. A plain push is rejected.
cards.explanation: Recovering usually means they reset to your new history, which deletes any local commits they had on top, or you both merge and keep a duplicate. This is why teams forbid force-push to main. If you must update a personal feature branch, git push --force-with-lease refuses the push when someone else has added commits you have not seen. Plain --force overwrites those commits.

cards.front: What is the difference between a fast-forward merge and a merge commit?
cards.back: Fast-forward moves your branch pointer forward when there is no unique work on it. A merge commit has two parents and records that two lines of history joined.
cards.explanation: git merge --ff-only fails instead of creating a merge commit, which is what you want when updating a local main that should only move forward. git merge --no-ff always writes a merge commit so a feature branch stays visible as a unit. GitHub's 'Create a merge commit', 'Squash and merge', and 'Rebase and merge' are three different histories. Squash puts the whole branch into one new commit and drops the intermediate hashes.

cards.front: What does a rebase do that a merge does not?
cards.back: Rebase replays your commits on top of a new base, producing new hashes and a linear history. Merge joins histories and keeps the original commits.
cards.explanation: git pull --rebase updates your branch by replaying your local commits on the fetched upstream, instead of adding a merge commit. Interactive rebase (git rebase -i HEAD~n) can reword, squash, fixup, edit, or drop commits. The Git book lists those todo commands. Do not rebase commits that already exist on a shared branch. You would be asking everyone else to rebase too. Rebase drops merge commits unless you pass --rebase-merges.
cards.example: git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main

cards.front: A rebase stopped with a conflict. What are your three honest options?
cards.back: Fix the files, git add them, git rebase --continue. Or skip this one commit with git rebase --skip. Or return to the pre-rebase state with git rebase --abort.
cards.explanation: Abort is always available until you finish, and it is the right call when the replay has gone wrong. continue will refuse if conflicts are still marked. Skipping drops that commit's changes entirely — only do it when the commit is already contained upstream. Leaving the repo in the middle of a rebase is why later commits look 'impossible'. Status tells you that a rebase is in progress.

cards.front: What do squash and fixup mean in an interactive rebase?
cards.back: squash melds a commit into the previous one and opens the message editor so you can combine messages. fixup melds it in and discards this commit's message.
cards.explanation: Use these to turn 'wip', 'fix test', 'fix test again' into one reviewable commit before you open a pull request. The todo list runs top to bottom and can be reordered. Reword changes only the message. edit stops after the commit so you can amend it. drop deletes it. This rewrites hashes, so do it before anyone else is using the branch, or coordinate a force-with-lease.
cards.example: git rebase -i HEAD~5  then change pick to fixup on the noise commits.

cards.front: How do reset --soft, --mixed, and --hard differ?
cards.back: --soft moves HEAD and keeps the index and working tree. --mixed (the default) moves HEAD and resets the index, but keeps your files. --hard moves HEAD and throws away staged and unstaged changes.
cards.explanation: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but leaves the changes staged, ready to recommit. That is the safe way to split or reword locally. --hard is destructive. Use it when you mean it: you have a copy of the work, or the changes were bad. It does not erase the commit object immediately. The reflog can still find it. reset on a shared branch that you then force-push is how teams lose commits.

cards.front: How is git revert different from git reset?
cards.back: revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier commit. History stays. reset moves a branch pointer and can discard commits from that branch.
cards.explanation: On a shared main, revert is the tool. The bad commit remains in history, and a new commit cancels its diff, so other people's clones pull cleanly. The Git revert docs say: if you wanted to throw away uncommitted edits, that is reset or restore, not revert. Revert can conflict if later commits touched the same lines. You resolve it like a merge.

cards.front: Why is reverting a merge commit a special case?
cards.back: A merge has two parents. git revert -m 1 <merge> undoes the change relative to the first parent, usually the branch you merged into.
cards.explanation: Git refuses to revert a merge without -m because it does not know which side is the mainline. After you revert a merge, Git records that those changes were undone. A later merge of the same branch will not replay commits that were already merged. The usual fix is to revert the revert, or to rebase the feature onto new commits and merge that. This is documented in Git's revert-a-faulty-merge notes and is a classic production surprise.

cards.front: What does cherry-pick copy, and what does it leave behind?
cards.back: It replays one commit's diff as a new commit on your current branch. The original commit stays where it was. The new commit has a different hash.
cards.explanation: Use it to move a hotfix from main onto a release branch without merging everything else. If the replay conflicts, cherry-pick stops, sets CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, and marks files the same way a merge does. Continue with git cherry-pick --continue or abort with git cherry-pick --abort. Cherry-picking a merge needs -m for the same mainline reason as revert. You can get duplicate changes if you later merge the original branch.
cards.example: git cherry-pick -x a1b2c3d   (-x records the source hash in the message)

cards.front: How do you get a commit back after a reset --hard that you regret?
cards.back: git reflog shows where HEAD has been, including commits no branch points at. Find the hash from before the reset, then git reset --hard <hash>.
cards.explanation: The reflog is local. It is not cloned and it expires (often after 90 days). This is also how you undo a bad rebase: the Git cheat sheet says to find the old tip in the reflog and hard-reset to it. If the commit was never in this clone, the reflog cannot invent it. Push to a remote is what makes work recoverable from another machine.

cards.front: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
cards.back: fetch downloads new objects and updates remote-tracking branches such as origin/main. It does not change your files. pull is fetch plus an integration: merge by default, or rebase with --rebase.
cards.explanation: Fetch is the safer first step when you want to look at incoming commits with git log HEAD..origin/main. pull hides that step and can create a merge commit you did not want. Many teams set pull.rebase true so a pull replays local commits. Either policy is fine if the whole team shares it. Confusing origin/main (a remote-tracking bookmark) with main (your branch) causes 'I pulled but my branch did not move'.
cards.example: git fetch origin && git log --oneline main..origin/main

cards.front: You are in detached HEAD. What happened, and how do you keep the commits you just made?
cards.back: HEAD points at a commit, not at a branch. New commits are not on any branch and will become unreachable when you leave. Create a branch now: git switch -c rescue.
cards.explanation: Detached HEAD happens when you check out a tag, a raw hash, or the middle of a bisect. Git warns you. If you already made a good commit, switch -c captures it. If you did not, just switch back to main. There is nothing wrong with detached HEAD during bisect. Forgetting and committing there is the hazard.

cards.front: How do conflict markers work, and what should you leave in the file?
cards.back: <<<<<<< is your side (HEAD, or the branch you had checked out). ======= separates the two. >>>>>>> is the incoming side. Delete the markers and keep the resolved text.
cards.explanation: During a merge, 'ours' is the branch you are on and 'theirs' is the branch being merged in. During a rebase, those names flip, because rebase checks out the new base and replays your commits on top. That flip causes a lot of wrong resolutions. Read the code. Do not memorize ours/theirs under pressure. After editing, git add the file. Merely saving it does not mark it resolved.
cards.example:
<<<<<<< HEAD
int timeout = 2;
=======
int timeout = 5;
>>>>>>> feature/slow-client

cards.front: How do you stash work, including untracked files, and take it back safely?
cards.back: git stash push -u -m "wip parser" saves tracked edits and untracked files. git stash pop applies the latest stash and drops it if the apply succeeds.
cards.explanation: A stash without -u leaves new files in the working tree, so the tree is not clean and you still cannot switch branches. pop can conflict. If it does, the stash is kept. apply is the same without dropping, which is safer when you might want the stash on two branches. stash is a pair of commits under refs/stash, not a separate kind of magic. Do not treat it as a backup. It is easy to drop.

cards.front: How do you find which commit introduced a bug?
cards.back: git bisect start, mark a bad commit and a known good commit, then test each checkout Git offers. Mark it good or bad. Git binary-searches the history.
cards.explanation: Bisect needs a reproducible test. Automate it with git bisect run ./test.sh. It checks out commits in detached HEAD. When it prints the first bad commit, git bisect reset returns you to the branch. A broken test that fails for an unrelated reason will blame the wrong commit. Skip untestable commits with git bisect skip.
cards.example: git bisect start && git bisect bad HEAD && git bisect good v1.4.0

cards.front: What should you look at before you push a feature branch?
cards.back: git fetch, rebase or merge the latest main, run tests, and read git log origin/main..HEAD and git diff origin/main...HEAD.
cards.explanation: Three dots in git diff A...B compares the merge base of A and B with B, which is the feature's own change. Two dots compares the tips and includes unrelated main movement. Reviewers use the three-dot form whether they know the name or not. Push the branch, not main. Open the pull request from that branch. If the branch was already reviewed and you rebase, say so, because every comment anchor may move.

cards.front: What does git restore do that people used to do with checkout?
cards.back: git restore --staged file unstages a file, leaving the working copy. git restore file discards unstaged edits in that file, replacing them from the index.
cards.explanation: Older guides say git checkout -- file to discard edits and git reset HEAD file to unstage. Those still work. restore and switch split the two old meanings of checkout, which is why new docs prefer them. restore --source=<commit> file can pull a file from another commit. It will overwrite local edits. There is no recycle bin.
cards.example: git restore --staged src/App.java && git restore src/App.java

cards.front: Why does a teammate's force-push make your local feature branch look wildly conflicted?
cards.back: They rewrote commits you already based your work on. Your commits still have the old parent. A merge tries to reconcile two histories that contain the same changes under different hashes.
cards.explanation: The Git rebase manual calls this recovering from an upstream rebase. If you have no unique commits, reset --hard to their new tip. If you do, rebase --onto their new branch from the last old commit you shared. This is the cost of rebasing a branch other people use. Prefer merge commits on long-lived shared branches, and rebase only personal branches.
cards.example: git fetch && git rebase --onto origin/feature old-base feature

cards.front: What is an annotated tag, and when do companies use one?
cards.back: git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "release" stores a tag object with a tagger, date, and message, pointing at a commit. A lightweight tag is only a name on a commit.
cards.explanation: Release tags should be annotated and then pushed explicitly: git push origin v1.2.0. A plain git push does not send tags. Tags are how you reproduce a deploy. Moving a tag that already shipped is another history rewrite. Sign release tags if the company requires a trusted build.
cards.example: git tag -a v1.2.0 <commit> -m "Fix payment timeout" && git push origin v1.2.0

cards.front: What does git blame tell you, and what does it not tell you?
cards.back: For each line, it shows the commit that last changed that line, and the author of that commit. It does not tell you who originally designed the behavior if a later commit only formatted the line.
cards.explanation: A rename or a reformat makes the last author 'wrong' in a human sense. git log -L or git log -p on the file tells the story. Blame is still the fastest way to find the commit message that explained a surprising line. Do not use it as a performance review.

cards.front: How do you undo the last commit but keep the changes unstaged?
cards.back: git reset HEAD~1 which is --mixed. HEAD moves back one. The files stay in the working tree, unstaged.
cards.explanation: Use --soft instead if you want them to stay staged. Use revert if the commit is already on the remote main. HEAD~1 means the first parent of HEAD. On a merge commit, ~1 follows the branch you were on, not the branch you merged, so read the log before resetting a merge.

cards.front: What belongs in .gitignore versus what should be removed from history?
cards.back: gitignore stops untracked files from being added. It does not untrack a file that is already committed. Removing a secret from the latest commit is not enough if older commits still contain it.
cards.explanation: git rm --cached file stops tracking without deleting your local copy, then commit that removal. For a leaked credential, rotate the credential first. Then purge history with a tool such as git filter-repo, and force-push every affected branch. Ignore build outputs, IDE folders, and .env. Do not ignore a lockfile the team needs in order to build the same dependency tree.

cards.front: A pull request has 30 tiny commits. What merge strategy keeps main readable?
cards.back: Squash and merge, or an interactive rebase that squashes before merge. Main receives one commit with one message. The feature branch's intermediate hashes stay only on that branch.
cards.explanation: Squash loses the ability to bisect inside the branch's tiny steps, which is acceptable when those steps were 'fix typo'. It is the wrong tool if each commit is an independent, buildable change you want to revert separately. A merge commit preserves all of them and adds a join. Pick the policy in the repository settings so authors do not invent a new history shape every time.
cards.example: On GitHub: Squash and merge. Locally: git rebase -i origin/main and mark fixup.

cards.text: git {{c1::fetch}} updates remote-tracking branches and does not change your working files.
cards.extra: git pull fetches and then merges or rebases. origin/main is the remote-tracking ref. main is your local branch.

cards.text: To undo a commit that is already on main, use git {{c1::revert}}, not reset.
cards.extra: Revert adds a compensating commit. Reset rewrites the branch pointer. Reset plus force-push on main drops other people's history.

cards.text: git commit --amend creates a {{c1::new}} commit hash.
cards.extra: The old commit remains until nothing points at it. Amending a pushed commit forces everyone else to reconcile histories.

cards.text: During an interactive rebase, {{c1::fixup}} squashes a commit and discards its message.
cards.extra: squash also melds into the previous commit but keeps both messages for you to edit. Commands come from git rebase -i, documented in the Git book.

cards.text: git push --force-with-{{c1::lease}} refuses to overwrite remote commits you have not fetched.
cards.extra: Plain --force will overwrite a teammate's push. Lease is the safer rewrite for a personal branch.

cards.text: git reset --{{c1::hard}} discards staged and unstaged changes.
cards.extra: --soft keeps them staged. The default --mixed keeps them in the working tree but clears the index. The reflog can still find the old commit.

cards.text: Reverting a merge requires {{c1::-m}} and a parent number.
cards.extra: -m 1 usually means the branch you merged into. Later merges of the same commits will not come back automatically.

cards.front: How do you see a compact graph of commits before you rebase?
cards.back: git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20 shows hashes, topology, and branch or tag names.
cards.explanation: Look for merge commits before a rebase. A default rebase will flatten them. If the graph is already shared with other branches, prefer merge. --decorate shows that HEAD, origin/main, and your branch may point at different commits even when the messages look similar.

cards.front: You staged too much. How do you stage only part of a file?
cards.back: git add -p walks each hunk and lets you type y or n. The commit then contains only the hunks you accepted.
cards.explanation: This is how you split a drive-by refactor out of a bugfix so the review stays honest. If hunks are too big, you can split them with s. After a partial add, git diff shows the unstaged remainder and git diff --staged shows what will be committed. Do not use add -p on generated files.

cards.front: What does a clean status actually guarantee?
cards.back: Nothing you care about is uncommitted, except files Git is not tracking because they match ignore rules. It does not mean the code builds or that you pushed.
cards.explanation: Ignored secrets and build folders will not appear. A clean tree can still be behind origin/main. Check git status -sb: it prints ahead and behind counts when the upstream is set. 'Your branch is ahead of origin/feature by 1 commit' means that commit exists only on your machine until you push.

cards.front: How do you update your feature branch onto the latest main without a merge commit?
cards.back: git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main while your feature branch is checked out.
cards.explanation: If you have already pushed the feature branch, the rebase rewrites those remote commits and the next push needs --force-with-lease. If the branch is under review, warn reviewers. If conflicts are large, merging origin/main into the feature branch is slower history but preserves the hashes reviewers already commented on. Both are valid. Rewriting a branch someone else is also committing to is not.
cards.example: git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main
